lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: The Overtaking Illusion
top_level_objectives: Observe and define the apparent retrograde motion of planets against the background stars.
Contrast the complex geocentric (epicycle) explanation with the elegant heliocentric explanation of planetary motion.
Understand and visualize how Earth overtaking a slower outer planet creates the geometric illusion of backward motion.
Compare retrograde motion properties across different outer planets to see how distance affects the illusion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the normal (prograde) motion of planets against the background stars from an Earth-based perspective.
key_visuals: A surrounding night sky dome featuring recognizable constellations (e.g., Leo and Cancer).
A distinct, bright red dot representing Mars.
A time-lapse user interface allowing students to advance time night-by-night.
student_actions: Locate Mars in the AR night sky.
Advance the time-lapse controls to watch Mars drift slowly eastward (prograde) relative to the background stars.

scenes.brief_purpose: Observe the core phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion in the night sky.
key_visuals: The same night sky dome with constellations.
A glowing trajectory trail that traces Mars's path over several weeks.
student_actions: Continue advancing time until Mars appears to slow down and stop.
Watch Mars reverse course (move westward), form a loop, and then resume its eastward journey.
Use an AR measuring tool to highlight the loop and note the duration (roughly two months) of the retrograde phase.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show the historical geocentric explanation to highlight its mechanical complexity.
key_visuals: A mechanical, clockwork-like geocentric model with Earth at the center.
Mars attached to a small circle (epicycle) which is in turn attached to a larger circle (deferent) orbiting Earth.
student_actions: Walk around the 3D geocentric model to inspect its nested circles.
Turn a crank to animate the epicycle model, matching the resulting mechanical loop to the sky loop observed in Scene 2.

scenes.brief_purpose: Transition to the modern, heliocentric view to set up the true explanation of the phenomenon.
key_visuals: A zoomed-out, top-down view of the inner solar system with the Sun at the center.
Earth and Mars on their respective concentric orbits.
student_actions: Scale and rotate the AR solar system to view it from a top-down perspective.
Play the orbital simulation to observe that Earth moves faster on its inner orbit and takes less time to circle the Sun than Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the heliocentric orbits to the Earth-bound observation to reveal the 'overtaking' illusion.
key_visuals: The top-down solar system view, now enclosed in a distant sphere of background stars.
A glowing 'line of sight' laser projecting from Earth, passing through Mars, and hitting the star sphere.
A picture-in-picture window showing the view from Earth.
student_actions: Manually drag Earth along its orbit until it approaches Mars.
Observe the projected laser dot on the star sphere.
Step slowly through the 'pass' to see that as Earth overtakes Mars, the changing angle of the sightline causes the laser dot to trace a retrograde loop on the starry background.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6: Further Out: Jupiter and Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how a planet's distance from the Sun affects the geometry and visual extent of its retrograde motion.
key_visuals: An expanded top-down solar system model that includes the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
Multiple lines of sight projecting from Earth through Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn onto the star sphere.
student_actions: Run the orbital simulation at a higher speed.
Compare the large, dramatic retrograde loop of Mars with the smaller, flatter retrograde loops of Jupiter and Saturn.
Identify that because Jupiter and Saturn are further away, the parallax effect from Earth's motion is smaller, resulting in less extreme apparent backward motion.
